# The EMI Fix

Listen

Share

> How an academic journal published a 1,200-word commentary that would help define the most important scientific debate of our time. Only problem: that commentary broke every single key publication rule.

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," width="800px" />

> _“A vocal minority of biased scientists free to spread misinformation”
By a WHO insider_

### Context:

In February 2020, while the WHO was still frantically negotiating access to China and to critical early data — three closely coordinated papers helped lock in the “natural origin” narrative:
(1) The Proximal Origin of SARS-CoV-2 (Nature Medicine),
(2) the Lancet Letter, or more properly the “Statement in support of the scientists, public health professionals, and medical professionals of China combatting COVID-19” (Lancet), and
(3) a commentary titled “No credible evidence supporting claims of the laboratory engineering of SARS-CoV-2 ” (EMI) — the least remembered of the three. This article shows exactly how the third one was assembled.
Based on my original thread, with new material.

## a1. The Storm

### The Plan

It started on 29 January 2020.

At that point, no one knew where SARS-CoV-2 had come from. Wuhan was locked down. Cases were appearing across the world. But on that day in January, Ralph Baric explained that SARS-CoV-2 may be a lab escape, or even be a man-made construct, in a classified session of the Biological Sciences Experts Group (BSEG) convened by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI).

That confidential meeting had alarm bells ringing through the US and UK intelligence services and their governments. Immediately after, in the UK, Farrar was tasked with doing a side-check of these claims. This triggered the Farrar call on 1 February, which would paradoxically be soon recycled into offering a supporting public narrative for the benefit of the WHO and its ability to get access to China.

Indeed, all of these events at the time were proceeding quietly behind closed doors. Neither the intelligence services’ concerns, nor Baric’s, nor the WHO’s actual motivations, were for public consumption. None of this was meant to be public. Too hot, too consequential while still uncertain, with nothing at all to gain from public exposure.

### The Clouds

At least that was the plan. But in these very same closing days of January, various articles were published, which highlighted that a research accident was a possibility and quickly picked up traction.

Some claims were easy to dismiss, such as the preprint posted on 31 January by an Indian research group that suggested unusual features in the virus genome. Some claims could not be dismissed on facts, being careful and logical, such as when Sen. Tom Cotton highlighted the possibility of a research accident in a letter to the US Administration on 28 January. A letter in which he correctly also asked for a suspension of flights coming from China to the US.

> Regarding this last point, I ask that the administration urge President Xi to allow American and international scientists and medical experts from the World Health Organization into Wuhan immediately to help treat infected persons and research the origins of this coronavirus.
> 
> If the virus didn’t originate in the seafood market, it’s critical to determine where it did — especially, I must add, since Wuhan is also home to a biosafety-level-4 super-laboratory that engages in the study of coronavirus, among other deadly pathogens.
> 
> source: letter from Sen. Tom Cotton, 28 Jan 2020

### The President is too busy

While the public discourse was getting rather volatile, Pres. Trump himself actually kept praising China, since he was more interested in trying to close some trade deal with that country, than in some weird new virus in Wuhan.

This left the initiative to the Office of Science and Technology Policy (White House) to try to activate the US academies to Chinese academies links, to seek cooperation on the origin issues raised by the new virus. This was standard ‘softer’ engagement via scientific institutions, called Track II in the diplomatic language. An approach that would also highlight a non-politicisation of the question under the aegis of the OSTP.

Thus, on 3 February, the OSTP (White House) sent a request letter to the National Academies of Science (NASEM). It asked one simple question: what data is needed to be able to clarify the origin of the virus.

Three of the scientists NASEM consulted were Peter Daszak, Kristian Andersen and Baric. Andersen tried to get the draft response to mention that the outbreak was ‘consistent with natural evolution’. Still — and very logically since an origin statement as offered by Andersen was not in the remit of the question asked — the final version of the answer to OSTP made no mention but also no denial of a possible research-related origin, it just concentrated on specifying quickly which data points would be useful.

## 2. Context: The February 2020 Lockstep

On 7 February, a team in Guangzhou dropped what looked like the perfect answer to the data point question that OSTP had just asked four days earlier. They had found a coronavirus in pangolins that was supposed to be 99% identical to SARS-CoV-2. At the time, it seemed that the natural origin case was closed before it had even really opened.

Nobody knew it then, but over the next few weeks, riding on the convenient back of that 99% claim, three papers would be published that would shut down this debate for years, while the pangolin ‘99%’ claim would be soon proven to be totally wrong.

In just 10 days, three coordinated publications locked in the natural origin narrative globally, starting with the two most famous ones: Proximal Origin and the Lancet Letter.

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

> _The manufacturing of a narrative in February 2020_

Proximal Origin and the Lancet letter were being drafted between 4 and 11 February, and their publication was carefully piloted by Farrar. The EMI commentary was started on 11 February, just as the other two were entering final review. All three were completed and published before any substantial data were publicly available.

The publication timing of Proximal Origin and the Lancet letter was particularly critical for the WHO; it had just managed to send a WHO team to China, which arrived there on 16 February, but without yet any firm agreement on access. Proximal Origin and the Lancet Letter were supposed to clear the clouds, signal to China that the WHO was not ill-intentioned, so that one could get back to the plan and the imperatives of health diplomacy.

## 3. The Commentary

This story is not about Proximal Origin. It is not about the Lancet letter. It is about the third paper. Yes, the EMI Commentary; the one that almost nobody remembers, maybe because — for once — Farrar did not have a hand in it.

On 11 February, Shan Lu, one of the three editors-in-chief of the journal Emerging Microbes and Infections, enlisted two friends: Shan-Lu Liu at Ohio State, and Lishan Su at UNC Chapel Hill (where Baric works). He asked them to write with him a commentary on SARS-CoV-2 origins. Over a few hours of work, the three of them came up with some draft , with Shan Lu (EMI’s Editor) playing an essential role in the shape and the content of the piece. By the evening of February 11th, they had a first draft ready, with Shan Lu’s name purposely not included as a co-author.

### Insight: The Mechanics of the “Fix”

The emails reveal a strikingly compartmented process. The Chinese editors maintained what one might call a walled Chinese dwelling (外封闭内开敞) — fully open internally, tightly closed to outsiders. The two Western co-authors were effectively air-gapped, kept unaware of Shan Lu’s central editorial role.

At the same time, Ralph Baric and Shi Zhengli appear as ghosts in the threads — consulted on content but never formally disclosed, despite their obvious conflict of interest.

In the end, every standard rule of authorship transparency and conflict disclosure was set aside.

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

Shan-Lu Liu sent a draft that same evening to Linda Saif, another senior virologist, with whom he had recently published an editorial [1]. She wrote back within the hour, wondering if she could share it with Ralph Baric, while casually adding that “I know he would not want to be a co-author.”

Baric is the most famous coronavirus researcher in the world. He invented the techniques that are used to engineer bat coronaviruses in laboratories. He had been collaborating with the Wuhan Institute of Virology for years.
He knew more about this subject than almost anyone alive.

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

> _Progressive additions of the Western token co-authors, 11–12 Feb. 2020, FOIA email excerpts_

And Saif, while proposing to send the commentary to him, knew that he would not want to take a public co-authoring role. This was a preference which under other circumstances could be justifiable, but which was strictly unethical given his obvious conflict of interest. The right thing to do would have been to refuse to have anything to do with the draft.

Shan-Lu Liu agreed with Saif that they should share it with Baric. Saif also suggested they send it to Peter Daszak. They did. He never replied.

Susan Weiss, another well respected virologist, was invited to join as a co-author a few hours later. As with Linda Saif, neither Shan-Lu Liu nor Lishan Su deigned to tell her that the editor of the journal was the one behind the commentary idea, and that he was taking a very active part in its writing.

Saif and Weiss were given the impression that they were joining an independent academic commentary. They were joining a narrative operation.

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," width="800px" />

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

> _Looping Baric in. All 4 disclosed co-authors listed on 12 Feb. 2020, FOIA email excerpts_

Very tellingly, Shan-Lu Liu and Lishan Su maintained carefully compartmented email threads: While Shan Lu, the EMI editor and hidden co-author, was exchanging many emails with Shan-Lu Liu and Lishan Su where they together edited the text, these last two never included him in any of their equally many emails with Susan Weiss or Linda Saif.

The whole operation was designed like a traditional walled Chinese dwelling (外封闭内开敞, ‘closed on the outside, open on the inside’): Shan Lu at the heart, Shan-Lu Liu and Lishan Lu on the inside, Weiss and Saif on the outside just like carefully positioned flower pots.

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

### Insight - EMI

A very Chinese publication
The journal of Emerging Microbes and Infections is part of the Taylor & Francis (UK) stable of scientific publications. EMI’s editorial office is based in Shanghai, at the address of the School of Public Health of the China Fudan University’s Fenglin Campus. That’s also where Shan Lu holds an adjunct faculty appointment, beyond his main job as a professor of Medicine, Biochemistry and Molecular Pharmacology at the University of Massachusetts Medical School (UMMS).

EMI started as a new journal with modest Impact Factor, rapidly climbed into the mid-6 range by 2017, experienced an exceptional (but temporary) COVID-driven surge around 2021, and has now settled into a solid Q1 position. It remains one of the stronger open-access titles in emerging infectious diseases/microbiology/immunology.

As of 2026, 2 out of the 3 Editors in Chief of EMI, 7 out of 8 of the Associate Editors, all the 10 Section Editors and 9 out of 12 of the review editors are Chinese or Hong Kong citizens.

At the same time Shan Lu, Shan-Lu Liu and Lishan Su (the three real authors of the EMI Commentary) all have key positions in US research labs and/or universities. Shan-Lu Liu was also the founding President of the 145-strong Association of Chinese Virologists in America (ACVA), which was created at the time of alleged profiling of Chinese scientists under the first Trump administration. In 2024 Shan-Lu liu was named President of the American Society for Virology.

The legal shell
EMI is published on behalf of Shanghai Shangyixun Cultural Communication Co. (上海上宜讯文化传播有限公司), a company set up in 2011 that has acted as a specialized vehicle for its publishing partnership (with Nature Publishing Group from 2012 to 2018, followed by a switch to Taylor & Francis).

As per per the Chinese company registry, Shanghai Shangyixun Cultural Communication Co. has two token directors, and the wording of its business scope is generic and general, ecompassing anything from: ‘the design, production, agency, and publishing of various advertisements, cultural and artistic exchange planning (except performance agency)’ to the ‘selling [of] advertising materials, clothing and apparel, leather products, shoes and hats, craft gifts, and electronic products’ [2]. This is typical for a company set up by a Shanghai company-formation agent, in anticipation of EMI’s creation and its first publishing partnership.

Whatever the run-of-the-mill declared business scope, the company has functioned exclusively as a specialized vehicle for handling EMI’s copyright, tax and local compliance for its international academic publishing partnership with Taylor & Francis. As a small private limited-liability company (一人有限责任公司), Shanghai Shangyixun Cultural Communication Co. is not required to, and does not, disclose any audited accounts.

## 4. The Ghosts

Baric got the draft at 8pm that night. He sent back detailed tracked changes by midnight. None of his contributions would ever be disclosed.

Shi Zhengli, the scientist who ran the coronavirus lab at Wuhan, was also sent the draft. She provided comments. No one would ever know she had seen it.

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

> _Reception of Zhengli’s comments, 16 Feb. 2020. FOIA email excerpt_

And then there was Shan Lu himself. The editor of the journal. He did not just commission this paper. He also shaped it and and actively co-wrote it. He waived the publication fees. He told his staff to accept it the same day it was submitted. He joked in emails about bypassing peer review.

And he insisted, over and over again, that his name should not appear anywhere on it.

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

> _Shan Lu boasting of having bypassed peer-review, FOIA email excerpt_

There was one reviewer. He did not ask for any changes. He just wrote one line: “Publish immediately. These are good people.” That is not peer review. That is a rubber stamp.

The four names that appeared on the final paper were just the public face. The real authors were sitting in the shadows.

## 5. The Beijing Lab-Accident

On 14 February, while the draft was still circulating, Shan-Lu Liu sent a short email to three people. He did not send it to Saif. He did not send it to Weiss. He only sent it to Lishan Su and Shan Lu.

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

> _Shan-Lu Liu email privately mentioning a SARS-2 lab-infection in Beijing, 14 February 2020, FOIA email excerpt_

> “Feng Gao is my old lab mate at the Beijing virus institute. My former director has just been infected with SARS-CoV-2 in a lab accident.”

This was dynamite.
The same institute had leaked SARS four separate times in 2004. They had covered up the first two outbreaks. And now, at the exact moment the world was arguing about whether this new virus could have escaped a lab, there had been another lab infection.

The authors did not disclose this. They did not even mention it. They added one vague line at the very end of the paper about general laboratory safety risks, and left it at that.

If this fact had become public in February 2020, the entire debate about the origins of COVID would have gone very differently.
They omitted it.

## 6. The Pangolin Deflation

The pangolin paper was supposed to end all arguments. But it fell apart within a week.

When the full data came out, it turned out the 99% similarity only applied to one tiny part of the virus. The rest was nowhere close. And most importantly, the pangolin virus did not have the furin cleavage site.

What is the furin cleavage site? It is the single most unusual feature of SARS-CoV-2. It is the reason the virus spreads so well between humans. And no close relative of this virus had ever been found with this sequence. Susan Weiss noticed this immediately. On 20 February, she wrote to Shan-Lu Liu:

> “Frightening to think it may have been engineered”

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

> _Susan Weiss clearly stating that the FCS may be engineered, while putting the final touch on the commentary that says the exact opposite, 21 February 2020, FOIA email excerpt_

She told them they could not dismiss the lab origin possibility. She told them the pangolin evidence was not enough.

They ignored her completely. The paper went to press unchanged, and she did not ask for any change. The line about the pangolins stayed in. The conclusion dismissing lab origin was not altered in the least.

Why? Because fact-based doubts are for private conversations between scientists; comforting zoonotic certitudes are what goes to papers and commentaries in scientific journals, so as to set the right safe official tone.

It’s not even as if there was any other option in their minds — there is no discussion at all about that public/private contradiction between them — that attitude is engrained, just as natural as breathing.

This may be the most shocking aspect of the story — but anybody versed in the institutional reality of chasing grants, chasing funders, and prioritizing scientific cooperation with China, especially in a tense political climate, will know that anything else was anathema.

## 7. Every Rule Broken

This was not normal scientific publishing. Every single standard was violated:

<img src="data:image/png;base64," width="800px" />

The paper was published on 26 February, exactly seven days after the Lancet letter. It had been submitted on 13 February by Shan Lu’s left hand, accepted the same day by Shan Lu’s right hand. That’s efficiency.

It was translated into Chinese before it was even posted online. It would go on to become one of the most read papers in the history of the journal, propulsing EMI up in the virological / epidemiological rankings for two years.

No one knew it had been largely shaped and written by the journal Editor. No one knew Baric and Zhengli had edited it. No one knew that the Chinese co-authors had air-gapped their two token Western counterparts so as to maintain the charade about Shan Lu’s role. No one knew the co-authors had hidden a lab accident. No one knew they did not even believe their own conclusions.

The emails obtained through FOIA by US Right To Know show all of this. They show exactly how it was done. And nobody really cares. Not Taylor & Francis, not Shan Lu or any of the co-authors. They all did very well out of this.

- Shan-Lu Liu was the President-Elect of the American Society for Virology (ASV) for 2024–2025, and its President since then (2025-). He is also part of the Subcommittee of Election of the American Academy of Microbiology (AAM) (2024-).
- Susan Weiss was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2023 and American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2025. She is President-Elect of the American Society for Virology [2025-]. Since at least July 2025, she is also a Board member of EMI (as are Christian Drosten and Linfa Wang).

## 8. Conclusion

### A never-ending spin

Today, the people responsible will tell you it was necessary. They will tell you there were crazy conspiracy theories everywhere. They will tell you someone had to calm the public down, clear the way for continued cooperation with China.

And now that the emails are public, they have a new argument. They say that pointing out what they did is itself the conspiracy theory.

Most recently, Florence Débarre, a French researcher at a state institution, wrote a long blog post arguing that anyone pointing out these documented facts is just ‘manufacturing outrage’.
To get to that beautiful conclusion, she first chose to ignore all the inconvenient facts, chose to focus only on Baric and Shi Zhengli roles, and then argued that there was no issue (the ‘manufactured outrage’) because — Abracadabra! — EMI itself has come out and ‘clarified’ that their contribution did not meet the level of disclosure [3].

This is the trick. They do not argue about the emails. They do not argue about the lack of peer review. They do not argue about the hidden lab accident. They just say you are crazy for noticing. They say that the people who lied in public are the responsible ones. And the people who found the lies are the cranks.

### Why this matters

This was not some grand conspiracy. It was smaller than that. It was sadder than that. It was a group of people who all knew each other. Who trusted each other. Who decided, in a moment of panic, that they knew better than everyone else. That the public could not handle the truth. That it was acceptable to cut a few corners, to hide a few facts, to tell a small lie, and even to play each other occasionally.

All for the greater good (health diplomacy) if one is generous, or for some more narrow good if one is realist (their own good), but in both cases against the background of some geopolitical trope that was influential at the time, courtesy of both the WHO and some domestic rancour against Trump (‘China good, US bad’).

It is worth remembering the genuine uncertainty that existed in early February 2020. Real genomic data were still scarce, the pangolin 99% announcement looked odd but promising for a short time. Many scientists — including some who later became more open to lab-origin hypotheses — genuinely believed a natural spillover was the most parsimonious explanation on the very limited evidence then available, and even more scientists recognised it as the only ‘safe’ explanation to align oneself with.

But the issue raised here is not that the EMI Commentary authors should have known the “right” answer with hindsight. In fact, they did not change their line a iota when the 99% claims came crashing or when learning of a SARS-2 infection in a Beijing lab; They already perfectly knew that the zoonotic certitudes they were professing at the time were unfounded.

That is how institutional decay happens. Not with a bang. Not with the traditional villains plotting in their corners. But with quiet, apparently respectable people, making what they know are wrong statements, and doubling down.

It is not clear whether the virus was manufactured by scientists, but it is absolutely clear that the consensus was. And that is just as dangerous. Because when this all came out, people did not just stop trusting those scientists. They stopped trusting all scientists. They stopped trusting all institutions.

Six years later, we are still living with the cost of that choice.

## Insight — A Vocal Minority of Biased Scientists

In October 2021, a WHO insider told some UK journalist that:

> “If Sars-CoV-2 comes from an artificial consensus sequence composed of genomes with more than 95 per cent similarity to each other… I would predict that we will never find a really good match in nature and just a bunch of close matches across parts of the sequence, which so far is what we are seeing.
> 
> “The problem is that those opposed to a lab leak scenario will always just say that we need to sample more, and absence of evidence isn’t evidence of absence. Scientists overall are afraid of discussing the issue of the origins due to the political situation. This leaves a small and vocal minority of biased scientists free to spread misinformation.”

Today, the prediction about finding ‘just a bunch of close matches across parts of the sequence’ holds perfectly, and a vocal minority of biased scientists are still allowed to poison the well.

### Notes:

[1] The short Editorial in the Journal Viruses, dated 22 January 2020, essentially considered “understandable that Chinese scientists cautiously released the identity and genome sequence of this new virus”, stated that the virus was zoonotic, and hoped that “scientific collaborations between the US and China, including the study of emerging viruses and infectious diseases, will continue unabated despite some turmoil in other aspects of the US-China relationship” in a thin reference to Trump’s trade positions towards China at the time.

[2] For those interested in these minutiae: ‘the design, production, agency, and publishing of various advertisements, cultural and artistic exchange planning (except performance agency), marketing planning, public relations consulting, business information consulting, corporate management consulting, exhibition and display services, conference services, and computer network engineering (except special approval), technical services and consulting in the field of computer science, selling advertising materials, clothing and apparel, leather products, shoes and hats, craft gifts, and electronic products’.

[3] ‘Abracadabra’ is likely derived from Aramaic, with suggested roots in the phrase “avra kehdabra” (“I will create as I speak”). Making things up is indeed what that self-proclaimed debunker does.
